ca_canyon_boulders.blurb: A tight cluster of sandstone boulders within the Stoney Point park in Chatsworth, on the north edge of Los Angeles, just northeast of Beethoven's Wall. It holds 22 problems that run from very easy up to a couple of hard testpieces, with most falling between V0 and V3. The rock is fine-grained and kind on the hands but brittle, so it is worth skipping the day after rain and letting the ground dry completely. Compact lines and a mix of cracks, corners and faces make it a handy stop for a short session.

ca_lower_tier_3.blurb: The Lower Tier is part of Boy Scout Rocks in Mount Diablo State Park, east of Danville in the East Bay. Sandstone faces hold 22 routes: mostly bolted face climbs plus a handful of traditional lines, with top-rope options too. Grades start with a couple of 5.7s, then bunch up from 5.10 through 5.12, with one 5.13. Climbing here is about balance, edging and delicate footwork rather than power. The rock is soft, so stay off it when damp and treat older bolts with some suspicion. Expect sun for much of the day on the main faces.

ca_wedding_rock.blurb: Wedding Rock is a coastal outcrop among the redwoods and ocean headlands of Sue-meg (Patrick's Point) State Park, north of Arcata. It is one of the park's four main climbing spots and is almost entirely traditional climbing and top-roping: 22 routes, most between 5.8 and 5.10, with a few harder lines up to 5.12. The cliffs are short, around 60 feet, and a few lines are bold, with sparse protection and exposed traverses. Expect cool, damp mornings, ocean breezes and shifting weather. Good for climbers who like small gear, solid rock and scenery over big numbers.

ca_larry_land.blurb: Larry Land is a sport crag in the Bowman Valley, in the Sierra foothills off the Interstate 80 corridor north of Truckee, directly beneath the south dam of Bowman Lake. Its 22 routes are nearly all bolted, with one top-rope line, and the grades lean hard: a lone 5.9, a few 5.10s, then a strong block of 5.11 and 5.12 with one 5.13. Expect steep, athletic climbing on good edges and granite faces. It suits strong sport climbers more than beginners, and the walk from the road is short.

ca_boulder_1_2.blurb: Boulder 1 is a large sandstone block in the Stoney Point park in Chatsworth, in the San Fernando Valley, near the south entrance off the boulevard. It carries 22 problems from very easy scrambles to a few much harder lines, with the bulk at V1 to V3. It is one of the most visited boulders at Stoney Point and gets busy on summer evenings. The sandstone is fine-grained and easy on skin, but it chips and flakes readily, especially when wet, so give it several dry days after rain.

ca_danger_rock_or_orange_buddha_rock.blurb: A beach boulder at the far end of the main bouldering stretch of Mickey's Beach, in Marin County near Stinson Beach. It has 22 problems, spread from V1 up to V10, with a good number in the V4 to V9 range, which makes it more of a strong climber's rock than a place for beginners. It is best when the sand has been scoured low, typically winter into late spring. Fog is common and a sunny day is usually breezy. Check tide levels before you go and bring a few pads.

ca_flavin_haven.blurb: Flavin Haven is a popular sport crag on a bend in the Upper Gorge of the Owens River Gorge, near Bishop in the Eastern Sierra. Most of its 22 routes are bolted single pitches, with two trad lines, running mainly from 5.10 through 5.11, with a few 5.9s, a handful of 5.12s and one 5.13. The gorge is cut in volcanic rock that gives edges and pockets. The wall is sunny and open with little shade, so it is a good choice for cooler months and a hot slog in midsummer.
ca_flavin_haven.approach: From the base of the upper-gorge descent trail, follow the gorge floor south, pass beneath the railroad trestle and continue around the bend.

ca_claim_jumper_wall_2.blurb: Claim Jumper Wall sits in the Central Pinnacles of Holcomb Valley, in the San Bernardino Mountains just north of Big Bear Lake, at roughly 7,500 feet. The 22 routes are mainly bolted, with a good number of traditional lines and one top-rope, graded from 5.7 up to 5.11, mostly 5.10 and 5.11. The granite is heavily featured, so harder-looking climbs often go easier than expected. The Central Pinnacles have the shortest walks in the area and draw crowds in peak season. Watch for rattlesnakes near the base in warm weather.
